spots.name: Karosta Prison
spots.label: Karosta Prison

text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so plan the visit on foot. The route is through the streets, so keep an eye on the map as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: Zemgales iela is a public street, but the prison and its yard may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Karosta Prison is in Karosta, a district of Liepāja.
text.description:
Karosta Prison is the red-brick prison building in Liepāja's Karosta area, with a watchtower close to the entrance. In the yard there are some striking outdoor exhibits: a military truck, a field kitchen and an amphibious vehicle. The yard is the one place where the building itself fills the frame, so it is the best choice for a classic picture of the prison.

It does not show the prison. Streets nearby, such as Zemgales iela, are a suggestion for a different kind of photo: weathered brick and Soviet-era buildings, many of them abandoned, which make moody, textured street pictures. Treat this area as a quieter extra stop, then walk over to the prison for the main shot.

At the prison, the red brick, the tower and the vehicles give you plenty to work with. Start wide to take in the building, then move closer for details such as brick texture, the tower or one of the vehicles. Photography is generally allowed in public areas, but check with staff about any restrictions, and confirm the yard is open to visitors on the day.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: On the street, use the lines of the buildings as leading lines and turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. In the prison yard, put one of the vehicles in the foreground and the brick building and tower behind it, so the picture has depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the red brick keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. Keep gridlines on to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out details such as brickwork or peeling surfaces. At the prison, the ultra-wide helps if you are close to the building and want the tower in the frame too.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Zemgales iela (walk through the streets near the prison, reached on foot). Abandoned, weathered brick and Soviet-era buildings in the street, a quieter alternative to the prison's own frontage; these are not views of the prison itself. From here the idea is to photograph weathered brick and Soviet-era buildings in the nearby streets, such as Zemgales iela, not the prison, which lies to the west. For the prison itself, go to the yard of Karostas cietums, where you can frame the red-brick building and the watchtower near the entrance, with the truck, field kitchen and amphibious vehicle in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight is best for the street and the yard. Soft, even light, such as on a bright overcast day, shows the brick texture without harsh shadows.

spots.name: Karosta
spots.label: Karosta

text.directions_text: From central Liepāja, head north into Karosta and ask for Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle (the Orthodox naval cathedral). Get to the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, in front of the main facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.access_note: The outside of the cathedral is open to photograph, but it is a place of worship and the interior is restricted, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
text.geographic_location: Karosta is a neighbourhood in the northern outskirts of Liepāja, on the Baltic coast, and covers about a third of the city's area. The cathedral stands among the district's blocks of flats.
text.description:
Karosta is a former naval base on the northern edge of Liepāja, and it is unlike the rest of the city. The base was built between 1890 and 1906 for Tsar Alexander III. Later it became a closed Soviet military town, and at its busiest more than 20,000 people lived here. The Soviet forces left in 1994, and much of the area was left to decay. Today it draws visitors and artists with its fortress ruins, old admirals' houses and rows of block housing.

The best single photo here is of the Orthodox naval cathedral, St Nicholas (Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle). Its golden onion domes and decorated facade stand out against the plain concrete apartment blocks around it. That contrast is the picture: ornate and gilded in the foreground, grey and plain behind. It also tells you something about the district's history in a single frame.

On a phone, keep it simple. Stand in front of the main facade, on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, and decide whether you want the whole building or just the domes. Include a little of the surrounding flats rather than cropping them out, because they give the scene its character. If you have time, two other spots in Karosta are worth a look: the canal at Oskara Kalpaka tilts, and the long North Pier, which has the ruined fortress behind it.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the domes and facade as the main subject, and leave a strip of the plain blocks in the frame so the contrast shows. Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the building does not lean. If you are near the canal, Oskara Kalpaka tilts gives a waterside view of Karosta as an alternative. The North Pier gives a different shot, with the long breakwater and the ruined fortress behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the golden domes to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the gold keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white. Step back and use 2x or more rather than tilting the phone upwards, to avoid converging lines.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade with some of the surrounding flats. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the building will not fit. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes alone against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main facade, Studentu rotas iela 7 side). The golden onion domes and facade of the Orthodox naval cathedral, framed against the surrounding Soviet-era concrete apartment blocks. Stand on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, in front of the main facade of Sv. Nikolaja Jūras katedrāle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear daylight shows the gilding best. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the domes.

spots.alt: Karosta, Liepāja: a former naval base on the northern edge of Liepāja. Photo spot

spots.name: St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral, Karosta
spots.label: Naval Cathedral

text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head north from central Liepāja to Karosta and check the map for your route. The phone icon on the map marks the cathedral itself. Once you reach the building, walk into the grounds in front of the main facade and step back a little so the domes fit in your frame. Check the entrance on the map, as the address is given as Studentu rotas iela 7 in some places and Katedrāles iela 7 in others. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The exterior and grounds can be reached on foot from the street, but this is an active place of worship and photography inside is prohibited, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Karosta, the former naval district in the north of Liepāja. It stands among the apartment blocks of the area, with its main facade on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side.
text.description:
St. Nicholas Naval Cathedral stands in Karosta, the former naval district in the north of Liepāja. It was built in the style of 17th-century Russian churches, with a large central dome and four smaller domes around it. The designs were by Vasily Kosyakov, and the church was completed in 1903 to serve the Russian navy based here. Its later history was rough: it was used as a gymnasium and a cinema in Soviet times, and it was returned to the Orthodox Church after Latvian independence, with the first service held in December 1991.

For a phone photographer, the main appeal is the outside. The golden domes and ornate walls look very different from the plain grey apartment blocks nearby, and that contrast makes a strong picture. Stand in the grounds in front of the main facade, on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, and you can fit the whole building and its domes in a single frame. Keep the walls upright by using the gridlines, and leave a little sky above the central dome so it does not look cut off.

The cathedral is an active place of worship and photography inside is not allowed, so plan to take your pictures from outside. Allow a few minutes to walk around the grounds, as the domes look different from each angle.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight. Include a strip of the grey housing at the edge of the frame if you want to show the contrast with the gilded church. Then take a closer shot of the domes with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the golden domes to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the gilding does not turn white against a bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole cathedral. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the domes will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the golden domes and the decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the grounds in front of the main facade on the Studentu rotas iela 7 side, a little way back from the building, so the domes fit in the frame. From here you see the golden domes and ornate exterior set against the grey Soviet-era apartment blocks nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunrise and sunset, when the low golden-hour light suits the exterior.
